utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. The Trial Chamber is convening today to hear the final arguments in the case of the Prosecutor against Mile Mrksic, Miroslav Radic, and Veselin Sljivancanin. We informed the parties that, for urgent and personal reasons, Judge Parker is unable to attend. Pursuant to Rule 15 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Trial Chamber has decided to hear the closing arguments in the absence of Judge Parker. Today we will first hear the closing submissions of the Prosecution. Tomorrow and Friday we will hear the Defence. The Trial Chamber has carefully reviewed the briefs and it will be greatly assisted by them. Prior to giving the floor to the Prosecution, the Trial Chamber wishes to draw the parties' attention to a question that was, in our view, not sufficiently addressed in the final briefs. This question concerns a point of law in relation to the charges of crimes against humanity. In order to constitute a crime against humanity, it has to be established that the attacks and commissions charged are part of a widespread or systematic attack directly against the civilian population. This is the chapeau requirement for crimes against humanity. The Tribunal's case law is very clear to the effect that the presence of noncivilians in the population does not alter the civilian characteristic. What could be open for argument, however, is the following: Is the question whether the victims of a crime against humanity were civilians are not relevant to the applicability of Article 5. In other words, is the general condition of the civilian status of the targeted population that is required for a chapeau requirement, is that general condition identical to the condition of the civilian status of the victims of the underlying crime? The Trial Chamber would like to have the views of the parties on this particular point. The parties may either answer this question immediately or, if they prefer, present oral -- brief oral submissions on this question on Friday after Mr. Lukic finishes his presentation on behalf of Mr. Sljivancanin. Okay. So the floor is now to Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I thank the Court and I'm glad to see that everyone is still here. It seems such a long time since I've actually stood at this lectern. May I just deal with some preliminary points that I submit are important. Firstly, there is clearly a problem, and that is that the problem is that the Court clearly is asked to judge a set of facts and attitudes 16 years after the event. The danger that that creates is that we often, unconsciously, apply the standards of today and we do not take into account the intensity of feelings which had been caused clearly here in what can be called an internal, or as I will call, a quasi civil war set of circumstances, where, unfortunately, brutality invariably raises its head. It is in our submission important to remember the timing that the Soviet bloc had just -- had ceased, but we are dealing here with forces who had been taught that war should be pursued in a ruthless way. In support of that submission, may I please place before the Court and my learned friends several small pieces of evidence to set the context of this case as a whole. The first, I hope, will be a video clip, the helicopter view of Vukovar, which was taken some years after the event. If that could be played, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We submit that this evidence clearly shows the extent of the destruction and the devastation brought upon this particular city and the civilian population. One just has to look at the number of buildings destroyed, the totality of destruction, the extent of the destruction. And as I say, this is, I believe, at least two years after the conflict had ceased in 1991. And this video quite literally does a full circle of Vukovar itself. We would submit that that demonstrates what the JNA may consider is proportionality when it comes to destruction; we submit that in no way demonstrates that. Vukovar was, as had been indicated in evidence, the Stalingrad of Croatia and that was its intention. I would like to also refer, if I may, and read from one short exhibit. I believe it's Exhibit 305. It was called the Babska declaration and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Moore, to interrupt. The exhibit number for the video shown, I don't think we got that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will just -- 317 I'm told. Thank you very much. I'd like to deal with the Babska declaration, and the Court may remember that Babska was a small village in Croatia, in eastern Croatia, and there had been a suggestion that individuals there had various weapons. By 4.00 - and this is paragraph 1 of that - the JNA gave the following ultimatum. "By 4.00, collect all the weapons in the village and bring it to Vikjaca where a body of the JNA will be waiting." And this is the part that we submit demonstrates that same attitude. "Insofar as this is not done, your village will cease to exist on a geographical map." And, again, I would submit that when you talk about this document and when you talk about the video that we have seen, it demonstrates a course of conduct that the JNA meted on Vukovar and the surrounding area and villages, which quite clearly was intent on destroying virtually everything it could lay its hands on. May I deal also with the attitude that existed in relation to these defendants. And I deal with Sljivancanin and Mrksic in particular. I'd like to deal, if I may, please, with a video-clip, and this is of Mr. Sljivancanin. We submit that it demonstrates not a man who sits today, as he did previously, perhaps 17 years on, like all of us, a little older, a little greyer, a little rounder, but a man who is -- and I would submit that he demonstrated arrogance, he demonstrated intolerance, he was a driven man, he was a loud man, and he demonstrated, I would submit, a hatred of the people who resisted him. May we play that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We can do without the sound; it's not necessary. The point that I wish to emphasise is one should look at the body language. This is not a man who is tolerant. This is not a man who is trying to compromise. This is an arrogant man. This is a man who is dictating to people who are there to help, and his body language clearly demonstrates that attitude. We have heard words such as "peacock." They may well be appropriated. It is not for me as a Prosecutor to suggest that. Of course the point in this video, as the Court is well aware, as one can see now that there are vehicles going over the bridge in behind. This is Exhibit 318, and the Court has seen it many times. I would like also then to play very shortly Exhibit 138. Again, the Court will remember Mr. Sljivancanin's words that Mr. Borsinger -- he and Mr. Borsinger got on very well. If this can be played.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That is not the look of a man who is willing to compromise. That is a gentleman who is treating Borsinger with complete contempt and any comments that Mr. Sljivancanin has made in evidence are disingenuous and false and we would submit that when you look at his conduct over the period of time, that in actual fact those words that I suggest are appropriate are, indeed, that. Two final pieces of evidence that I would seek to rely upon, just to create the context of this case, is a document which is Exhibit 312. The Court may remember it. It was Mr. Kypr. It was created on the 8th of November, 1991. It was a compilation of the ECMM documents or ECMM reports, where they were dealing with the issue, geographically, as a whole. Clearly it precedes Vukovar and cannot be applied to that extent, but, in our submission, the Court is perfectly entitled to look at other witnesses who have given evidence, if they consider that documents are reliable, their compilation is reliable; they can look at the content and draw such conclusions as they deem appropriate. In paragraph 6 of the second page, it reads as follows: "The JNA systematically denied any guilt referring to the armament of the population and the provocative behaviour from their side. The assumption that the population was armed is mostly true. It appears, however, that compliance with the ultimatum never changed. The further course of events." And then the following: "Attacks with tanks, artillery, and armoured infantry against the unarmed or slightly armed villagers, this in itself should be considered a violation of the generally accepted humanitarian principles of proportionality and subsidiarity." And the next part we submit is highly apposite when it comes to this case. Another defence of the JNA was that they could not be held responsible for the behaviour of the Chetniks. "The monitor team is, however, convinced that the JNA very closely cooperated with those reservists and is of the opinion that the leadership of the JNA should directly or indirectly be held responsible for their acts." I would submit that this is one week before when Vukovar surrendered. I would submit when you look at that and in conjunction with other matters, it demonstrates, as I say, a complete attitude of the JNA towards people that they consider, as we have heard, terrorists and criminals. And then finally this. I ask the Court just to bear in mind the evidence of Ambassador Okun. He gave evidence on many topics. Most of it is dealt with in our brief which is I hope fairly comprehensive and extensively footnoted. But one can look at Okun and ask oneself what kind of a man was he. Was he a man who had judgement? Was he a man who could assess individuals? Was he a man who could assess situations? And he was asked what he thought of Mrksic when he came across him. And this is the evidence that he gave. It's at transcript 1766. He had described Mrksic as military correct but hard. "Q. How did you come to the conclusion that he was hard? What did you mean by that? "A. 'Hard' is a polite way of saying brutal and I came to that conclusion by his manner, by his manner: The briefing, the strutting, the attitude, highly belligerent, not towards us. His general military bearing, as I said, was quite correct, but it was also quite clear that this was a hard man." Because it does take there to be a hard man to commit the crimes that were committed at Ovcara. In the Defence brief, I believe of Mr. Lukic, at paragraph 334, he indicates the following. "There had been a clear plan that persons who were a potential danger for security of the implementation of the evacuation of wounded and sick for which there had been a reasonable suspicion that they had participated in armed actions be separated and, via the barracks in Vukovar, be transported through Sremska Mitrovica." We agree with Mr. Lukic. There was a plan, but the plan was not as he states. The plan was to identify, it was to isolate, it was to control, it was to remove secretly, but not because of security but because these individuals had been classified as criminals and terrorists. And we would submit that the intention as such, should and would be that they would be treated differently. The Court, I suspect, will remember such phrases from individuals where phrases like: "They will be swallowed by the dark," "you're not going to need those," when there was reference to Dosen and his personal items. We say that that was an indication of the very clear intention of what the JNA and their subordinated units were going to achieve. There was a clear intention to persecute this group of Croats and non-Serbs, and we submit that it can be gleaned from the evidence. It can be gleaned by words expressed, it can also be gleaned by lies told. And we submit lies have been told in this case by these defendants and witnesses who have come to give evidence, apparently truthfully, on their behalf. We can judge it by actions done. We can also look at such things as absence of lists, contrary to much military doctrine that has been set down in stone. And finally, by the targeting of specific individuals. In my submission, it begs the question. If there was concern for the security of the evacuation, it means really one of two things. Firstly, this alleged or expressed concern for the security of the convoy could not be guaranteed from the threats of severe violence from the local Vukovar TO. The Court may remember that. Or, secondly, that these were desperate men who may have had intentions to escape, bearing in mind that they were supposed to be terrorists and criminals. But we submit that if there had of been a genuine explanation, a genuine fear, then why would you only put two armed guards on the buses? We would suggest that it is the first part of the plan, that it was intention to deceive individuals, that nothing would happen to these parties. The second part of the plan, because we, as I say, say there is a plan, is evidence that is often forgotten, and that is the evidence of the grave-digger himself. And may I just remind the Court of that evidence. That was P017. He said that soldiers from the JNA had been at the Yellow House since September. Therefore, we would submit, there was clear control of that area by the JNA. It was clearly in the zone of the responsibility of OG South. P017 was asked to dig a hole approximately 2.30 to 3.00 because that was the time he was finishing work. Timings here are extremely difficult for obvious reasons. It's often useful to try and use dark or night and day. His evidence was that he saw four or five buses stationary there. It begs the question, where does that place Vukasinovic's evidence, a main witness called on behalf of the Defence, because Vukasinovic said they came in three by three. That was not the case of the grave-digger who said that he saw four or five there. He said that people were just starting to get off the bus. He said also that the person who asked him to dig a hole was JNA. He couldn't say if it was an officer, but he said the following, he said that he was clean-cut, he was very neat, he was very tidy, he was clean-shaven, and he believed that he had an officer's belt and pistol. The Court has had an opportunity of hearing the method of dress of individuals, of TOs, and of this guards' regiment, the elite of the JNA itself. I would submit the following. The timing is probably accurate, that there were four or five buses is consistent with crime base witnesses; that he saw people starting to get off the first bus; and that it was a JNA-uniformed officer who asked for him, not a TO officer. What, therefore, can one glean from the digging of the hole? I would submit the answer is perfectly obvious, that there was an intention to kill which had been created and formulated by, at the latest, 2.30 that afternoon. Why else would you want to dig a hole? Please also remember what was said in evidence. The JNA officer said to him, It's enough. Let's drive back. The hole, apparently, was something like 10 metres by 3 metres; the dimensions are in the evidence. And secondly, there was an indication that he should return to cover the hole the next day. Again, I would submit if that evidence is accepted it clearly shows what the intention was at that time. On the way home he took the key. When he returned, the vehicle had not moved. The question I ask the Court to consider is this: Who covered the hole? Because we have heard evidence, have we not, I think from two sources, that in actual fact the JNA had heavy machinery at that time and there had to be, I would submit, a plan to cover that hole itself. He also said that there were a lot of soldiers and that he returned to his home nearby somewhere between 3.45 and 3.50. Again, perhaps important for 7(3) consideration, although that is not the main drive of the Prosecution case, that there were rumours the next day that people from the bus had been killed. Therefore, we submit his evidence is perfectly clear. There is an intention to kill. The buses four and five in number were there. The timing was at 2.30 to 3.00. The dimensions and the size of the hole, I still would submit, are important because clearly the Court will bear in mind the warning order of the 19th of November in the diary, the war diary, of the 80th, because there there was the warning order of 200 people coming from the hospital. And one should ask themselves the following question: How many people were actually taken from the hole? And in actual fact there was 198. Is it just chance? Is it just coincidence that 200 are mentioned the night before? 200 from the hospital, 200 from the same group who were murdered. Does that itself not perhaps suggest that there was an intention to kill clearly even earlier than has been suggested by myself this morning. Additionally, it also suggests that the grave-digger was under the control of a JNA soldier. The hole was covered. It was controlled by soldiers, and the rumour were occurring, as I say, the next day. So, in our submission, we have a plan to collect and to corral people called criminals and terrorists. The Defence, of course, say differently, but we say that the plan was one and the same and I hope by looking at the evidence and by drawing sensible and proper inferences that they will be shown to be the same. Now, may I also deal with one other matter. Much has been made by the Defence, not only in cross-examination, but also in their briefs, that in actual fact there were individuals who were feigning injury or wearing white coats. It clearly occurred, but surely the starting point must be as follows. Why should people behave in that way? We would suggest when you look at the evidence it clearly demonstrates that these were people in the hospital who knew and anticipated what their likely fate was going to be. And who is to blame them from donning a white coat or a false injury? Is it not to be said that their assessment was correct? Is it not right to conclude that it was the TO and the JNA being victorious that these persons in the hospital concluded that they would be killed? Is it not a proper and appropriate inference to be drawn in relation to that conclusion? Firstly, it was based on the TO and the JNA having control over the hospital and the people inside. Secondly, it is a reasonable inference that the JNA would either facilitate or participate or both in the persecution of these individuals. Thirdly, and extremely significantly in our submission, that the presence of the monitors would not succeed in stopping the crimes being committed against them. That belief was correct. That there would not be isolated killings but involve anybody who was deemed to have participated in opposing the JNA. And finally, in any event, the wearing of the white coats provided no assurance of safety, as many were killed who wore civilian clothes and indeed some had evidence of having received medical intervention or treatment and still were murdered that night. One of the issues that my learned friends, in particular Mr. Lukic, deals with relates to the issue of identification. I had the great pleasure of reading the Limaj judgement, and can I just deal with one or two aspects of it. Clearly, there was specific reference to the case of Turnbull and I'm sure my learned friends are well aware of it and also the case of Kupreskic. It is right and it is proper for a Court to consider that these are areas of difficulty. I accept that fully. I have been brought up on Turnbull and I'm afraid know it only too well. Of course a Court must exercise care, but is it not also right to say, that where a case against an accused depends wholly or substantially on the correctness of one or more identification, the Judge correctly should examine carefully the circumstances. And I ask the Court to examine the circumstances and to examine the evidence of the witnesses who were present at the hospital and other locations. How long did the witness see the accused or have the accused under observation, not merely in view? At what distance? What light? Was it an impeded view? Had he seen the accused before? How often? Had there been any specific reason for remembering the defendant? How long and what time interval between the sightings and the recognition, because in this case, there is identification and recognition. And I would equally submit that recognition is more reliable than identification of a stranger. And I ask the Court to bear in mind the recognition by Vezmarovic of Karanfilov and I will come to that in due course. I also submit that lives are something that can be looked at. If a Court views or takes a view that a defendant or a person has lied on a topic and the Court comes to the conclusion that that witness has lied, not for any other reason, but in recognition of his guilt, the Court are perfectly entitled to take that into account in corroborating any evidence of identification, and indeed other evidence as such. With regard to Mr. Sljivancanin, I would submit there are two important elements. Firstly, physically. Mr. Sljivancanin has been described by one of the Defence witnesses as so tall, so brave, and so handsome. It is not for me to draw any conclusion in relation to that analysis; however, he is a physically distinctive man, he is 192 centimetres tall, there or thereabouts, he had a distinctive moustache. Please bear in mind, in our submission, there has been a suggestion that Vukasinovic might have been the man that they picked out. Mr. Vukasinovic conceded and accepted he did not have a moustache when he was in Vukovar at the relevant time. Mr. Sljivancanin has a distinctive voice; therefore, we would submit, by his very physical appearance, he is very distinctive and stands out in a crowd. I don't have to repeat that. It may be said, Well, if he's distinctive, people can sometimes jump to conclusions. Well, that may well be the case, but when one looks at the totality of the evidence of the identifying witnesses, I would submit that that does not apply. Also, let us look at the conduct. As I've already said, he's a man with a loud voice, he is arrogant, he is condescending, he invariably seeks attention, he did not avoid it. If there are two words to sum up Mr. Sljivancanin, they are the following: I am. I am the commander. I am in charge. Mr. Sljivancanin, I would submit, was a man who was courting publicity, not avoiding it. And he was speaking to people in a way that made him all the more obvious. We accept that there is recognition from television and other sources, but there is also the counterbalance of people who were identifying. I ask the Court to bear the following in mind. Did those witnesses have reason to pay attention to him and did they have reason to remember him? Now, may I then conclude this part of my submission in the following way. I submit it is not only the individual identification of Sljivancanin, but also the cumulative or totality of the evidence that is sufficient to prove the appropriate or required standards, both for Sljivancanin and later on Karanfilov. The evidence of identification cannot and must not be viewed as if it is- and I use other words drawn from other judgements- hermetically sealed. It is the accumulation of all the evidence relating to a topic or topics which must be considered. Your Honours will be thrilled to know, I'm sure, that I have got a number of folders for them, and may I just pass them forward. My learned friends will be given theirs. What I intend to do -- I have a the file which has got the grandiose title of identification and I wish to go through the evidence of each and every witness that we say identified Sljivancanin at the hospital and also deals with the nature of the conduct and the level of control that he exercised. I will just ensure that the Defence will get them now. While those are being handed out to the Defence, may I just try and indicate how this is created. It's not exactly too difficult. What we have endeavoured to do is we have extracted identification of individuals who say they saw Mr. Sljivancanin at the hospital. One can see at the very top a box; in it, is included what we say are relevant points. The Defence can add to it, they can detract from it, they can do whatever they want to it, but it's there to help. With regard to the actual content and this is what I call a warts and all bundle. There is highlighting in relation to various sentences for what we say is important. This document has been created to assist the Court in relation to identification evidence, for speed you can see on the left-hand side the transcript references, and also the various references. The first witness is Polovina. One can see at 2588:5 the selection process, men to the left. As we move further down, the answer is: "Can you describe to the Court this man that you saw? "A. Yes, I can. He was tall, slim -- on the slim side. He had a moustache and dark black hair." Now, does the Court and my learned friends have they got that -- that part? There's nobody who's got anything in error. Then there was a question about her husband. She said about 180. And 2580 she said the man was taller and 2580:16: "A. At the time when I saw him for the first time, I didn't know his name. In the next 15 minutes or so while talking, whispering to the women standing around me I learned that his name was Veselin Sljivancanin." And then later on she said that several women had talked to him. May I draw the Court's attention, please, to 2581. This was where Polovina actually asked what was happening and he said: "Don't you worry, they are going for a brief questioning to the barracks and they, the men, will follow you soon thereafter." Dealing with this briefly, I submit that's a lie. It was a lie told quite deliberately, as lies tend to be, and it was there to ensure that there would be no problems with regard to the removal of the men. In relation to the identification there is reference to the moustache, tall, and thin. There is no suggestion in the evidence at all of any other person being at the hospital who fitted the same physical description, and the mere fact that Sljivancanin's name was whispered, we would submit, bearing in mind he introduced himself on a number of occasions and I will draw the Court's attention to it, does not of itself mean that the evidence is unbelievable. Can I ask the Court then, please, to go over to page 2, 2700:7, at the very bottom. There have been some cross-examination by Mr. Lukic about whether this was a valid identification or not. And I, on my customary hobby horse, had asked quite simply whether in actual fact the Defence are going to say it was him or it was not. And Judge Parker said the following: "Mr. Moore, if no Defence counsel pursues that issue, the expectation is that it is not disputed." This is a matter for the Court, how they deal with it, but it was never suggested that this witness was lying. And this, we would submit, is a recurring theme. But the important point is that there is a clear description of Sljivancanin himself. The next page 4 is P009. Again, he says he's described him at page 6122, described as a real, real officer, officer in charge." At 6122: "I mean that he was distinctively different than any other person that was around him. He was -- he had that real kind of look as a military officer, a JNA military officer." Then at 612213: " He was a very tall person in camouflage uniform -- with a Tito hat on his head. He had a brief-case or a bag that usually the officers would wear." And then at 25 and 26 one can -- as one moves down the page about hair colour. "It was dark hair at that time. He was a very tall person. I noticed a moustache." Again if one turns over the page at 6185 there is reference to the fact that he said that: "I found out it's Major Sljivancanin." Now, there is significant cross-examination on this witness, and I have no doubt at all that you will be addressed about it. But nevertheless these are independent witnesses, they are not people who have gone off in the same bus or were very close friends. There is an element of neutral corroboration. Next witness P031, and I believe there are 17 witnesses in this bundle. P031, I would submit, was a credible witness, came across as careful. At 3240 he said: "At that time a major of the JNA was in charge of the entire operation. Everything transpired under his control and on his orders." Clearly issue of command and control is an important element whether it be de facto or de jure. Here is a person looking at this man and saying that everything went through him. He said later on that he heard his name was Sljivancanin. At 324011: "When I left the camp and arrived back in Zagreb, in Croatia, then on a TV report -- in a TV report I saw that same major and recognised him as Sljivancanin. That major issued orders to his soldiers. He seemed to be a very arrogant officer." Again, the question at 3240:20: "Did you see any other officer in JNA uniform at that time? "A. At the time, I didn't see any other JNA officers." He did, however, refer to a lieutenant three lines down at 23. At 3247:3, the following question was asked: "Did anyone get off that bus before it left the hospital area? "A. Yes. There was a call being shouted. I just heard this. Just outside the bus I saw Mr. Sljivancanin." At the bottom of the page you'll see how it flows on, at 3248:23, about the hospital identification card. "Yes, I did confirm that. I left the bus afterwards. I got off the bus, and I addressed Major Sljivancanin. I didn't know his name at the time. I just knew he was a JNA major." And then it goes on -- the discussion, and I would submit that is entirely appropriate for the conduct of Sljivancanin that day. At 3250:10: "Did anyone give any order for the buses to move? "A. Yes. An order came for the buses to drive on to the barracks." This order was being issued by Sljivancanin. So I will not go through any other parts; they are highlighted. However, after significant cross-examination by Mr. Lukic, page 9, 3374:7: "Now you assert that the officer in question was my client, Veselin Sljivancanin. Is that correct? "A. Yes." And I would submit that in actual fact, when you look at the evidence of this witness, that he was a good witness, he was an honest witness, he gave credible evidence, and he is just another person who said that Sljivancanin was there. Page 10, P007 is an important witness. He's an important witness because the starting point is: "He introduced himself as Major Sljivancanin." So here is the introduction himself. At 4006:12: "In my opinion, these were regular soldiers of the Yugoslav People's Army." Just blow that: "He introduced himself as Major Sljivancanin and said: Now you will be transported to the Velepromet warehouse where you will be separated according to what was agreed." Now, this was Velepromet, this was the 19th, not the 20th. Later on at 4007:4 the Court can see that Sljivancanin said people would be taken to Velepromet. "After that he turned around, went down the steps outside the hospital, and spoke to two people wearing white uniforms. I did not hear their conversation, but I heard his voice telling one of those people to go back to their own country and issue orders if they like because he is in charge here." And the Court will remember very clearly the reference to Sljivancanin telling Borsinger to go back to his own country on the 19th. And then the description that one has down at the very bottom 4115:19: "He was tall, dark, good-looking. Everything became quiet as he introduced himself: I am Major Sljivancanin." And I would submit that 007 is an important witness, not only for the 20th, but also for the 19th, where there is an area of dispute. The next witness Bucko is important because it demonstrates not only the identification of Sljivancanin, but it demonstrates the coordination and the cooperation between the TO and Sljivancanin himself in what I will call the re-selection process. It deals with the morning of the 20th. If you just look at the very bottom, 2814:20, he's already said by this stage that he spoke to Sljivancanin but this was Ivankovic replying that he was no longer in charge. These men were now in charge. And when he said "these men," what did he mean? He meant the gentleman Major Sljivancanin. "What he said? He said, "You think you're any better than the rest of them." Now, may I just ask you again to move to 2826, number 23: "Did you eventually get off the bus?" Because he had been on the bus and was coming back. "Mr. Sljivancanin came, and Bogdan, the doorman, and another. Major, I don't know him but perhaps I would recognise him if I saw him again. And then they said, 'Get off.' You used to be soldiers." Bogdan almost certainly is Bogdan Kuzmic and Bogdan Kuzmic was a member of the TO who was being used at that time along with Miroljub for what I will call the re-selection or filtering process where Sljivancanin, by his own admission, was involved. At 276 he said: "Mr. Sljivancanin asked Bogdan whether he knew me, whether he recognised me." Then clearly the answer was that he had not and he was told to fuck off. May I draw the Court's attention then to 2831:3. "Now, you have told us about two meetings with Major Sljivancanin. "A. Yes. "Q. How do you know the person that you were referring to was called Sljivancanin? "A. Ah, that was nice. He came, I don't know when. It wasn't the first time on the 20th. He had to be at the hospital on the 19th because people were already saying things about him at the hospital, what he was like, that sort of thing. People were saying that he had introduced himself upon arriving there." And I would ask you to bear in mind the evidence of 007 in relation to that. "And can you -- can you describe to the Court the person that you called Sljivancanin? Can you tell us the height? "A. Very tall, wears a moustache, very tall, quite a strong man. He was strutting like a peacock, and he kept talking." That's at 2831:21. So I would submit that that witness is very important in relation to confirmation of Sljivancanin's attendance on the 19th, confirmation of introduction. He describes him. Of course it can be said it is retrospective, but you have reference to Bogdan, Bogdan Kuzmic I will submit. It was a re-selection process and we will see later on, with one other witness, the criteria that they were using for selection. I'm going to jump the next witness who is Dr. Bosanac not because she is not important, she's extremely important, but I just draw the Court's attention to one or two parts. There is page 68 -- sorry transcript 683:17. That is on our page 16. She said that she thought she spoke to Sljivancanin about 5.00 or 6.00 p.m. She then said that she spoke to him again that evening with Borsinger. Page 17, at 687:12, she said she first gave the copy to Borsinger and the remaining copies to Sljivancanin. There's reference to where she said: "I'm not going to go into that if I may." But could I ask you, please, just to look at page 18, our page 18. This relates to the interview that she had clearly at Negoslavci. It's at page 689:16 or transcript page 689:16. And here she's being asked about the discussions at the table. "The other man seated next to him," that was Sljivancanin, "said that I should watch my mouth because they had other methods to -- they knew for a fact that I had to know all these things because they had been listening in to all my conversations, phone conversations with Zagreb." And I am submitting that it is absolutely plain as a pike staff that there would have been notice of negotiations for the evacuation what has often been called the Zagreb Agreement. There's reference in her evidence about -- that it was Sljivancanin saying that she should assemble the medical staff, not any suggestion of Vujic, but it was Sljivancanin who was doing it. And then 855:15, our page 19: "When giving testimony on that day, the 19th of November, my client, Mr. Sljivancanin, first came with the soldiers in the afternoon hours and then once again in the evening around 1700 hours together with a representative of the ICRC. Do you remember that? "A. Yes." That evidence will fall into place, I hope, when we move on. The next witness is Kolesar. Kolesar, really the important part of Kolesar's evidence is on our page 22 at 953:15. She's talking about Sljivancanin. I don't think there's any dispute that it was Sljivancanin. "And then she told that he should write up a list and that was done very quickly, and the list was turned over to Mr. Sljivancanin. "A. Later on in the yard, I never saw Mr. Sljivancanin. I only saw him in the surgical clinic. We listened to what he had to say. We listened to him. So we saw him as a person addressing us, telling us something, the person of importance..." And at 956:21: "It was my impression that with everything that was going on there he was actually the person issuing orders and telling people what to do." I won't deal with P021, but I would like to deal with Vilhelm who links with Bucko on what I will call the re-selection process where the TO with Miroljub are involved. We say Miroljub was there at the beginning and he was there at the end. 4876:5: "When we arrived back at the hospital we were ordered to get off the bus. Our wives for waiting for us, or whoever it was who told us to bring our people back to the hospital. We lined up at the ready." 4876:17: "You told us that you were ordered to get off the bus. Who ordered you to get off the bus? "A. I don't know who did, but it must have been one of the soldiers, I assume. Also because Major Sljivancanin was nearby. "A. I had never seen this comrade, as they would say in the army, at all. I first set eyes on him when I arrived in Zagreb. It was then I first learned that the man's name was Sljivancanin. However, my wife had begged him to help us and she was the one who told me that that was Sljivancanin. "Q. Are you able to describe to the Court the height of the man that you say was Sljivancanin? "A. As tall as I am. Perhaps even taller, give or take an inch or two. Thereabouts. He wore a moustache, a uniform, a cap. "Q. And when you saw this man that you call Sljivancanin, were there any other soldiers with him? "A. He was with Miroljub Vujovic and Darko Kovacevic, a man known as Drko." And then there is reference to military uniform. We submit that Miroljub's presence is extremely significant. Our page 25, top off, 4877:16. "A. When we were lined up there was Miroljub and there was Major Sljivancanin, and they asked each man individually whether they were ideologically suitable. Miroljub was pointing fingers at people and he kept saying, 'This one, this one, and this one,' and those people would be released. When he came to me, he said that this man had been loyal to a certain month of the year but that me and my sons were Ustashas, and it was at this point that I was ordered to get back on the bus." Just below that 4878:25: "Miroljub would point people out and these people were free. They would join their wives and go on other buses. They went one by one, those who were released." Just below that: "All those who Miroljub Vujevic believed to be Ustashas were taken to one side and sent back to the bus." Again, just below that, again, 4879:9: "A. Miroljub told the major that I was an Ustasha and I was sent back to that bus. At this point in time my wife pleaded with Mr. Sljivancanin, Major Sljivancanin to let me go, because I was no Ustasha she said. She pleaded with all the Serbs she knew and they said, 'Maybe tomorrow.' But my wife knew that that would be too late." I submit again that the reselection process is very important because it demonstrates quite actively how Sljivancanin operates with Miroljub. The Court will remember at 9.00 at night when we're talking about the withdrawal of the military police at Ovcara, that Miroljub was also seen there in the presence of Karanfilov, who clearly is a direct subordinate of Sljivancanin. You have got Miroljub being involved at the start, you have got Miroljub's presence at the barracks, and you have got Miroljub involved at the end. I would submit that there is clear evidence of a continuity of plan and participants in that plan with regard to Sljivancanin and subordinates of Sljivancanin. I will not deal with P012 as we move on in time. This is P030 at page 30. If I deal with it very briefly, this is where there is reference to Captain Radic. Much issue has been taken of that, and I am sure that he will be -- have dealings with it. He says that he saw Sljivancanin by way of identification on the television, that he had seen him, that he saw him, I think, for approximately 15 minutes. He described the height, at least 190 centimetres, maybe even a few more, so quite high, quite tall, a quite tall up-right standing man, quite a presence. The next page at 9733, "He had an authoritative attitude, issuing orders letting us know that he was the main person there. Nobody dared interrupt him. He was the main figure in that area, standing in front of people, and he was issuing orders." I will not deal with page 32, P006, except to say that there is reference to lists of names in relation to him. May I then go to page 34. This is Berghofer. I would submit that Berghofer again is a very good witness, quite precise. First question. "Q. May I just deal with the man that you have described? Can you remember if he was wearing uniform or not? "A. He was so remarkable and striking that I wouldn't forget him even if I lived for another 50 years. He was tall, a strong man, he was wearing a soldier's cap, a uniform, a life jacket, and he had a moustache, and he was so striking that I don't think it's possible to forget a man like that." He then goes on to say halfway down the page that he saw him arguing on the bridge and we clearly have got evidence of that and no one is going to be suggesting that that's Pavkovic. At the bottom of the page, at 5279: "Well, it was shown on the news as well, and he was always referred to as Major Sljivancanin. And so it was quite clear that that was the man who was in command at the hospital." He was a hundred per cent sure. The following page, I'm not going to go into it, they are highlighted. There's reference to command by Sljivancanin, the control of the civilians and the buses. Page 36, four-fifths of the way down the page, at 545023, when there was an element of cross-examination he said: "Well, look, Sljivancanin is the kind of man you could spot from miles away; that's how tall he was." And then I believe this may have been a question from Judge Parker because of the reply, but I can't be certain of it. But here is the question anyway. "I'd like to deal with the hospital, please," that's at page 37, 5472, "I'd like to deal with the hospital, please, and the morning of the 20th of November. You have told us that you saw a man, tall man with a moustache, whom you believed to be Sljivancanin. All right? Did you see any other person who was similar in description and, namely, tall with a moustache, who was issuing you orders at any time? "A. No, Mr. Judge, I didn't. He was remarkably tall. He had a remarkable moustache. He is not a man one is likely to forget that easily." Again, when one looks at the evidence as a whole, a very clear picture emerges. Could I ask the Court, then, to move to page 43, and I will return then to page 38. The Dosen family clearly were killed or murdered at Ovcara, two members of them, and there is one other missing, I believe. But clearly Dosen was a name well-known to the TO and the JNA. And this is L. Dosen. She says quite simply that she "turned to look at the other buses and I spotted a tall officer with a black moustache wearing a camouflage uniform. I didn't know at this time who this person was. I just walked towards him, and I heard him being addressed as Major Sljivancanin." Just further down the page at 3801:13 there's a reference about her husband being on a stretcher. She said: "Yes, it's my husband." "Yes, I know that, but who specifically? And I said, 'Martin Dosen.' And then he said, 'Oh, it's Dosen.' I gave him a strange look, wondering how on earth he knew who Martin Dosen was. And then I said, 'Well, yes.'" 3802:1: "And then he was lost in thought for a moment, and then he raised two fingers to some two soldiers standing there in order to tell them to go back bus and bring Martin on the stretcher back. I thought at this point that they would take him back to the hospital, but they just left him lying in that corridor passage that I marked with the C. I asked Sljivancanin right away, 'I have Martin's bag on me containing his personal belongings and clothes. What I am supposed to do with it?' And he said, 'Well, the -- why would he need that?'" There's a slightly different interpretation of those. 3802:3: "A. I noticed him issuing orders, giving out commands, and that everybody reported to him, addressed him. And one could clearly see that everyone came to him, be it the reservists or the soldiers. If anyone had any questions, they all turned to him." There's issues of subordination, whether he has effective control, whether it's de jure or de facto. This is a woman whose husband is clearly of significant concern to her. I would submit that that is a situation where she herself would be well aware of what was going on, concerned for her husband, and when you hear her using phrases like "orders," "commands," both "reservists" and "soldiers," I would submit that it's entirely consistent with the way the Prosecution put its case. Again, if one looks at 3803:25: "A. I believe he was the commander there. I also took into account his insignia, because I used to be married to an officer. I could recognise rank and I knew he was a major." And later on she says "knowing he was a JNA officer, and seeing him in command." At 3805:2 she was talking about Chetniks and locals, and then it starts: "And I thought to myself, He was the only person to turn to, since he was commanding there, and if he should decide for me to go on that bus, so be it. Otherwise, I still need to try something." At 3805, and I'll leave it at that, at 3805:9: "The soldiers around him were calling him Sir or Major and they told me, 'Yes, this is Major Sljivancanin.'" That's at page 44. The reason I went slightly out of order because when I ask you to go to page 38, that's her daughter and some of the answers link to the mother's evidence. It's at page 38, and one can see that the first part relates to the 19th of November. "A. Major Sljivancanin came in through the door and introduced himself," again another person who says that he introduced himself, "he said he wanted them to leave those rooms and he left two regular JNA soldiers there to stand guard at the door. And he no longer allowed any of those others outside." Just below that: "He was wearing a JNA uniform. He was tall, slender. He wore a moustache, black moustache, black hair. He had some sort of cap or something on his head. And he clearly introduced himself, 'I am Major Sljivancanin.'" She also gave evidence for the 20th and that's why she is an important witness. 3918:9: "I saw Major Sljivancanin again," and this is on the 20th, "he was standing there with some soldiers issuing instructions to them, telling them what they were supposed to do. We just walked past, so I didn't hear what it was he was telling them." Just below that at 3918:17: "Q. And were those soldiers wearing uniforms? "A. Yes. All of them were members of the JNA." I won't go into the next page in any great detail apart from the top where there is a reference to: "I am Martin Dosen's wife," at 3923:4, because this is clearly the same account as her mother gave evidence on. And it says 3923:5: "And he said, 'Hmm, I see. Martin Dosen, why isn't he on the bus?'" And just below that: "'He will not be needing those things anymore.'" And the mother had said that she said spoken to Sljivancanin. There have been suggestions that they had colluded, at page 41, at 3978:18, because the suggestion of course is that they had colluded to point a finger at Mr. Sljivancanin, that their evidence was false or fabricated. She said: "We don't really talk about it very often. The images that still haunt me and all the things I remember can never be changed. Even if I discussed this with my mother, what I experienced, what I said and heard back then, I'm not saying that I can't be wrong about details, but all these images that will stay with me cannot be changed in any way. My experience was one thing; my mother's experience was a different thing altogether." I would submit they have reason to remember and you have got evidence of introduction, you have got evidence of identification the following day, which is recognition of identification, and that it correlates also with the identification on the 20th and the 19th themselves. Page 46 I will not deal with. There is evidence about Major Sljivancanin again being in charge. However, 49 is Zlogledza. This witness gives really two batches of evidence and is important, not only for the participation at the hospital but also at Ovcara. And if the Court wants to mark the top of page 49, "See also page 58," that may assist you to correlate the two transcripts. Zlogledza saw Sljivancanin twice, saw Sljivancanin at the hospital several times for periods of five to ten minutes, and secondly at Ovcara for 10 or 15 minutes, speaking with the TO outside the hangar. Initially describes Sljivancanin as quite tall, and you can find that on the first page, 49, at 10182:16. "I saw a man wearing a camouflage uniform. He was in and out of the hospital all the time." If my memory serves me correctly, that corresponds with the evidence of Karan, who, in his evidence, actually said that Sljivancanin was in and out on several occasions. I've not looked at that for about three or four months, but if my memory is right, I think that is correct. It then goes on at line 21: "He was quite tall, black hair, and a black moustache ... "Q. Did this man have any facial hair? "A. Just the moustache. "Q. What type of cap ... "A. A camouflage one ... slender. "Q. Did you know that person's name? "A. Yes. Sljivancanin. "Q. How did you know his name? "A. While we were still in the Vukovar police building, we were able to watch TV." Well, again there is significant cross-examination in relation to it. It's for the Court to come to their own conclusion about the credibility of the witness. It doesn't necessary follow because somebody has been seen on television that in actual fact that identification is wrong. There is a large amount of evidence to suggest that this witness was accurate. And it cannot be said that every witness is mistaken and every witness is a liar, as seems to be the case. Again, there is reference to seeing press photographs of Sljivancanin after the war, that he avoided any TV programmes about Vukovar, and perhaps one can understand why; that he didn't know about the film footage of Borsinger and Sljivancanin, and you have the reference to that. And then there is reference to the line-up and we can see that it is transcript 1028:2 and 1028:9. Clearly the Court are going to have to look at Zlogledza's evidence carefully because he says that Sljivancanin is at Ovcara. He is not the only witness who says that he saw Sljivancanin at Ovcara. The Prosecution case does not have to rest on the fact that Sljivancanin was present there. We submit that he clearly is part of the joint criminal enterprise to persecute these people, and indeed it is not necessary for him to be there, because he himself has been in charge of the evacuation in other ways and has a continuing influence and control over it. But I would submit that if Zlogledza's evidence is correct, then it puts into very clear perspective what Sljivancanin has been saying, because when one remembers of the interviews, in January and December 1998 before the judges, there was clearly reference to Sljivancanin saying that he had gone to Ovcara but he had got the days wrong and that he was there with Vukasinovic, I believe, to check on cars. One begs the question of what a man who is supposed to be involved in a security organ of the guards motorized brigade is doing at Ovcara, whenever it is outside the zone of responsibility is another issue and whether in actual fact Mr. Sljivancanin would ever really be there in relation to cars, but Zlogledza's evidence is something that clearly is going to have to be looked at with care. Page 53, and I will finish this before the break, is P032. He again is another witness who gives evidence about the 19th, and this witness says that in actual fact he had been given a lift by Sljivancanin when he, the witness, was on his way to the hospital. And it was a description at 3027:1: "He had a camouflage uniform, he was tall, and sported a moustache and he had a Tito cap with a red star on his head." And then there's reference to how he identified him, that in actual fact he had recognised him from a picture as he said perhaps a few days before the Geneva Conventions arrived is the way he described it. But again, we have got other evidence of Sljivancanin being at the hospital on the 19th, and if that's the case, this is entirely consistent with the evidence of other witnesses. Page 55 again is an important witness, 009. This witness sees Sljivancanin not only here at the barracks, but also at Ovcara. And if the Court want to write down -- see also page 57, which I think actually is the next page but one, it links on those two topics. At 6141 there is the description - I'm not going to go through it again. It's interesting. He said at 11: "He made a huge impression on me as an officer and a gentleman. He looked a real, real officer." Later on he says quite simply that he was a real, real officer, and there was a reference to the person that he saw. We say that clearly that it was Sljivancanin and that he was pretty much face-to-face with him at 6146:25 on page 26. So you have an identification, we submit, of Sljivancanin at the barracks. At page 57 we have got that he had cited Sljivancanin at Ovcara, that he had been seen at the hospital on the 19th. I'm not sure that's correct. And let me just check that, if I may. Thank you very much. If I may just locate that. Yes. That he had seen him at the barracks, that's right, where they had basically gone by, that he had also seen him at the barracks, as I've already referred to. At 6164:19: "And you said that you started walking slowly back around the hangar towards the entrance on your way back did you see anyone? "A. Yes, I saw the same JNA officer that I had seen at the hospital and at the barracks." I am submitting that it may well be that you can make an error once or you make it twice, perhaps, or it could be that you work upon a false premise. But clearly if this identification is right, it is the same person who is at Ovcara at that time. And at 6283:13 he said: "Before going over there I didn't see any officers at all. Coming back I did see Major Sljivancanin." And then there's the reference about -- that he was a major and how he had expressed various views to him. And then finally Zlogledza, as I said, there is the reference to how he had identified him. That was at page 48. This is where he said he had seen him at the hospital, at Ovcara. He had been in and out of the hospital and that in actual fact that he had watched Serb TV reports and that he had seen them on Serb reports from their TV stations, "I saw him on TV." I've tried to do it as briefly as I can and I've jumped and left out rather large traunches of evidence and it is rather turgid and I apologise for that. But the only reason that I do it is this. We are now, in 2007, much of the evidence was in 2005, a long time ago, and it is important to bear in mind, actually, some of the evidence that was given by way of identification. As I say, identification is evidence that one has to be careful about, but I would submit collectively and individually you have got identification of Sljivancanin on the 19th, you have got introduction of Sljivancanin on the 19th, you have got identification by way of recognition on the 19th and 20th, all at the hospital. The Court should be asking itself: What was this man doing? I'm submitting that he was utterly in control. This is not just a man who was responsible for triage because one clearly has to look at other evidence. And this is a man that everything he was going through with regard to the barracks with regard to Ovcara, that is entirely a matter for the Court on those identifications. But the one thing that is absolutely certain in our submission is that Sljivancanin, by his own acknowledgement, was there. And if these witnesses are to be believed, he was controlling absolutely everything at that time. And entirely consistent with powers given to him by his superior, Colonel Mrksic. It is now quarter to 4.00 and I think that is the customary time to adjourn. I will move on to other topics and try and work within the timetable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. We will have a break of 20 minutes now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I know time will be the enemy of this submission, I suspect everybody's submission, but what I have done is I will try and conclude Sljivancanin in half an hour. To assist the Court again, I'm sure you'll be thrilled to hear that I've got some other documents. One is in relation to exhibits and what I call a route map of our submission and I hope that this helps. I've also got it for my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I hope that there should also be a file. The Court should have that as well. May I explain the system that I hope to operate, and I underline the word "hope." The soft-leaf document which is stapled really are the closing submissions in very brief outline. Our case is in the closing brief, but these are parts where we try and deal with issues that we submit are very important, and there is then the file itself which particularises the exhibits that are already in evidence. If one looks at the schedule, it's perfectly obvious what they are, tab 1, the exhibit, the description, and the date which perhaps isn't so important. What we have also tried to do for speed is to highlight the actual section or paragraph. So, for example, if we go to just tab 1, one can see that it clearly is a series of regulations, but if you go to page 4 at the bottom we will be referring to Article 6, and Article 6 I hope will be highlighted. Thank you very much. And we have tried to do that through each and every document to assist. I'd like to deal with, if I may, with what we will call Sljivancanin's de jure and de facto control over the evacuation. In relation to the de jure powers, clearly Sljivancanin was put in charge of the hospital evacuation by the delegation of Mrksic; we say for two reasons. Firstly, the doctrine on the delegation of authority, as well as, the evidence put forward and evidence in relation to it from both Prosecution and Defence. The brief number for Prosecution is paragraph 523. When we talk about doctrine, here the powers relating to the command and control such as the hospital evacuation, we submit, can be delegated to a subordinate such as Sljivancanin. Really two points. The first point is that there is extensive evidence. The references are there for the brief, paras 524, which demonstrates Vukasinovic's appointment to be in charge of Negoslavci and 525 where there's reference to Sljivancanin being in charge of Mitnica, Velepromet, and the hospital. And so we would submit that that is an important element, that indeed he could exercise command responsibility prerogatives, based on the powers of the commander that the commander has delegated to him. Can I ask you, please, to look at tab 1 that I have already dealt with and that is under Article 6. It may well be I'll have to skip some of these exhibits because of time, but there, under Article 6, "The commander may authorise certain officers from the command to command units and institutions of branch services." Now, again in tab 2, we have got the reference to the delegation. At page 28, we can see on tab 2, page 28 which we have extracted, and it's in the notes in any event, that: "A commander may delegate some of his duties and obligations on the chief of staff, his aides, staff organ and subordinated commands." So we would submit that is the doctrine, that is the basis. And OTP brief 526 and I'll call it just 526 from now on. "The delegation of an operation by a commanding officer to a subordinate officer clearly does not diminish the commander's obligation to ensure a successful completion of the task and the subordinate officer's being delegated the task will not be absolved from his responsibility and will have," and the phrase is taken from Pringle: "Absolute authority and absolute responsibility to carry out the order assigned to him in the manner ascribed by his commander and remain responsible and accountable to his commander for the proper conduct of the task." I see the Court seems to be concerned. Is there anything I can assist the Court with? May I deal then with the second limb, which is evidence. It's Prosecution brief 553. The Court clearly remembers Vujic's evidence, the reference that Major Sljivancanin said the hospital would be vacated according to an evacuation plan that he, Sljivancanin, would personally be in charge of this mission. 554 of the brief, according to Panic, if Panic is to be believed, "Sljivancanin was present at 1800 hours at the OG South briefing." We submit that's extremely important evidence. "Mrksic put Sljivancanin in charge of the evacuation, allowing him to use Paunovic's military police." It's a fact, of course, that Paunovic denied. The alleged final destination of the buses was Sremska Mitrovica. And, therefore, in the conclusion that we place before the Court, is that Sljivancanin was put in charge of the evacuation from the hospital to its final destination and he was specifically given authority to use the military police for that purpose. Moving on to the briefing at 8.00 in the evening, 2000 hours on the 19th of November, the security organ briefing. Sljivancanin did not mention that at all in evidence, a little surprising one may think, but his subordinates did. The subordinates themselves were issued specific assignments and we can see quite clearly what those assignments were. Karan was to participate in the triage, to assist Sljivancanin in preparing all the security aspects of the evacuation. Vukasinovic to lead the transport. Karanfilov, who clearly played a key role ordering Vezmarovic to withdraw from Ovcara on the evening of the 20th. The order to stop at the barracks on the -- was issued on the 19th by Sljivancanin to those subordinates, and it was not a joint decision with Vujic taken on the 20th of November as Sljivancanin had testified. The Defence point, which we now deal with, is that the barracks were secure. We submit that's complete and utter nonsense. The barracks were not secure and it was not a secure place to stop vehicles who had terrorists and criminals inside. There were broken fences which surrounded the compound. There were clearly inadequate forces to protect the detainees. The proximity to the barracks -- the barracks to Velepromet, in our submission, is startling because there had been repeated incidents reported to Sljivancanin and Mrksic about maltreatment and abuses, the previous nights on individuals, and I ask the Court to just reflect on who was in charge of Velepromet. I seem to remember I think it was the 10th of November. There was the appointment of Borisavljevic, who was a subordinate to Sljivancanin, and clearly there was a direct link of the security organ into Velepromet a very short distance, I think five minutes' walk, perhaps 500 yards I seem to remember was the figure, and there was no logical or military reason for the buses to stop at the barracks. They had already been to Ovcara. They could have been gone to Ovcara straight away if there was a concern because Ovcara had been chosen for security. And the other thing is quite simply this. There was absolutely no reason for them to stop at the barracks. They could have gone straight through to Sremska Mitrovica because they were leaving early that morning and the buses were not expected at the barracks; we've heard evidence about that. And Susic was obliged, as a matter of urgency to provide protection for them. And therefore, we submit the following: Firstly, that there was, as I say no logical or military reason for the buses to stop. I've already dealt with that. And secondly, Sljivancanin due to his responsibilities over the whole evacuation had the obligation to evaluate and to assess potential threats involved and should have considered the risk that would have jeopardised the evacuation in any event, if he were a man who had genuine concerns for the welfare of those people. Dealing with de facto powers. I want to deal if I may please, at the hospital during the -- what we will call, the unlawfully evacuation. The brief numbers are 564 -- 562, 604 and 605.
