But it is quite clear that Sljivancanin, if he was at that briefing, was in a position to be aware about the information given to Mrksic by Vojnovic. Dealing with his presence at the various sites of the evacuation, we would submit is entirely consistent with the commanding role over all the evacuation. And in relation to subsequent knowledge of Sljivancanin about the killings, that is our paragraphs 610 and 611. We have the evidence of Hartmann on the 18th of November, 1992, during the celebration of the fall of Vukovar. Hartmann had spoken to Sljivancanin, "What happened in Ovcara one has to bury the bodies somewhere." That is completely denied. I don't know what people's views are on Hartmann or journalists, whether in actual fact she came across as a credible witness, I would submit yes. If in actual fact he did know and he was a participant, as we allege, then it is a perfectly obvious comment to make perhaps if Court unawares and with regard to Vukasinovic and clearly there was a close relationship between Vukasinovic and Sljivancanin. Vukasinovic, himself, said that the rumours of the killings were circulating around Vukovar on the 21st of November the next day. That was just one day after the event. And Vukasinovic's deputy had reported to him: "Boss, we heard that the people from Ovcara disappeared overnight and they were taken away to be liquidated." We of course know that Vukasavljevic gave evidence that he had informed the security organ but they did not want to do anything and that relates to tab 31 which I'm not going to refer to. Those would be the points that I would seek to refer to in relation to Mr. Sljivancanin. And I'm not finished with Mr. Sljivancanin, but I have for the time being,. But may I then move on with the Court's leave -- may I move on then please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, before you do, I have a question to put, not to put you off track here. It may be that I'm misremembering, but there seems to be information that General Vasiljevic from the department of defence was present in the evening of the 20th and had some dealings with Mr. Sljivancanin and also in that context a information from him that one should try to spare the maximum amount of prisoners of war in order to secure a future exchange between them and prisoners from the other side. I would like to hear -- it may be that had you thought to come back to this, but I would like to have now your comments on that, if that is contested; if not how that plays into the wider scheme of things as the Prosecution sees it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If my memory is correct in relation to the Mitnica evacuation, Sljivancanin was shown a telegram by -- I think from Vasiljevic and showed it to Vukasinovic saying, What do you make of that? That was the first dealings with Vasiljevic at that time. The second evidence was in relation to Karanfilov, who I believe from memory said that there had been an argument between Vasiljevic and Sljivancanin on the 19th where there had been, I will use my words, raised voices between them. The Prosecution's position would be as follows. It is impossible to know exactly what was occurring at that time. I will not speculate, but in our submission it is deeply unusual for an officer who is of major rank to be raising his voice towards Sljivancanin, towards a superior officer like Vasiljevic in the presence and hearing of others. One of the interpretations that is capable, is that Sljivancanin strongly disapproved of the order that Vasiljevic had given and that he had seen on the 18th, but there was no reference as far as I can recollect that Sljivancanin in his evidence said that he tried to apply that requirement of Vasiljevic when it came to the collation or the collection of the individuals who were going to be taken to Sremska Mitrovica. We are not able to say one way or other. The only matter that we find and we submit is unusual is his reaction on the 18th to Vukasinovic and his reaction and argument with Vasiljevic on the 19th. I'm afraid I would not be able to take it any further, and the Prosecution cannot take a definitive stand on that one way or other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Thank you. You satisfied my need. Thank you, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure which way to take that but I will try and avoid it in any event. May I move on, please, to Mr. Mrksic. We have applied the same principle with Mr. Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, I think there may be an error. The only thing that the Court should have should be the file, should be nothing else. No, that should not -- I don't know why that has happened. May I have it back? I had prepared for various eventualities and I will try and deal with it now expeditiously. Can we just count that the Defence have sent them all back. May I just deal then with Mr. Mrksic. Exactly the same principle applies. I've tried or we have tried, others have tried, to try and pick out documents and parts that we submit are important. The starting point is that Mrksic's position was that he was clearly the commander of the Guards Motorised Brigade and he was commander of Operations Group South, that started on the 8th of October, 1991. In relation to tab 1, Exhibit 591, you will find it there. I suspect it is not necessary but Trifunovic gives a very clear indication of what it is. He said that: "The zone of operations was taken over by the Guards Motorised Brigade and the command of the Guards Motorised Brigade transformed itself into the command of the Operations Group South and the then-commander, Mrksic, was appointed as commander of the Operations Group South." That comment, by Trifunovic, applies equally to Sljivancanin as it does to Mrksic. Our second point is that Operations Group South was a temporary formation. It related to the Guards Motorised Brigade, 80th Motorised Brigade, Territorial Defence, and various volunteer units. And the period of its duration was until the 23rd of November when he signed his last order as commander of OG South, and that is tab 2. There is no need, perhaps, to deal with that. Could I ask you, please, if you would be kind enough to look at tab 3, because there is one of the important topics which relates to resubordination. The time is 600 hours in the morning, and it relates to the resubordination of the Leva Supoderica volunteers and Vukovar TO and that's signed by Mrksic, and that clearly is after the killings and clearly the Guards Motorised Brigade was the chief force within OG South. Vukasinovic and Trifunovic said in actual fact that it was quite clear that Mrksic had uncontested control of OG South and that his command was never challenged. Indeed, that never has been an issue in the trial itself. With regard to de facto -- de jure duties. The brigade commander has: "The exclusive right to command all brigade units and attached units." That is tab 4 and it relates quite specifically to that. Secondly, tab 5 relates to delegation -- that a commander can delegate authority to officers subordinated to him. However, he cannot delegate the responsibility for the situation in the units and, this is the important point, remains responsible for their actions including those resulting from this delegation. And one can see under tab 4 and tab 5 in relation to brigade rules where that is actually specifically referred to and marked up. Again, dealing with delegation of powers, the delegation of an operation by a commander officer to a subordinate officer would not, in our submission, diminish the commander's obligation to ensure a successful completion of the task. That was Pringle who gave that evidence at T 11051, and I quote him: "The commander is fully responsible for everything that happens under his command, by those under his command, and in his area of responsibility." And in order to be able to exercise command and control, a brigade commander has to know the situation of the companies of his battalions, because otherwise the brigade commander cannot issue orders to these battalions." That was evidence given by Theunens at 10715. It's axiomatic, is it not, that under tab 6 that you have the obligation for humane treatment of wounded and captured persons, and we will deal with that issue, I hope, on Friday. A commander is obliged to report a crime to his superiors or initiate an investigation. That in our submission is important. Clearly we have got JNA regulations on that under tab 7, if I could ask you to be kind enough to turn that over. Because that is Articles 21 and Articles 36. The obligations that are placed upon him, and again he has a duty to protect captured members of enemy forces, which is Article 51 of that same code of conduct. Therefore, the Defence assertion that Mrksic himself cannot order his military police to investigate is flawed. We submit it has no merit at all, and that is paragraphs 55 to 59 of the Mrksic brief. And as indicated by a military police commander who gave evidence before the Court, namely Paunovic, the Guards Motorised Brigade commander had direct control of the military police. May I deal with the issues of his de facto command and control. Trifunovic, at 8113, said that: "The commander of OG South was informed about all important questions." And we would submit that when you look at our brief, paragraphs 86 to 89 it was perfectly clear that the commander, namely Mr. Mrksic, had a well-trained and functioning, efficiently functioning system for executing command and control functions themselves. Pringle, when asked to look at it in the perspective of command responsibility, command and control, at T 11034, he said as follows. "... it's clear to me that there was a functioning command and control system with information and orders flowing down the chain of command and information flowing up the chain of command, and that's exactly what I would expect." And the other matter that we would seek to pray in aid, at this point, is that the war diary, which clearly recorded the most important features and orders, reports sent and received by OG South, indicates that between the 1st of October and the 23rd of November there was clearly a functioning command -- functioning chain of command and reporting system between OG South and the superior and subordinate commands and units. That is Exhibit 401 for the Guards Motorised Brigade war diary. The OG South command briefings were clearly on a daily basis. They were attended, obviously, by Mrksic; his Chief of Staff Panic; his assistant chiefs, including Sljivancanin; as well as all the subordinate commanders. During those meetings, which is perfectly logical, subordinate commanders reported to Mrksic and they received tasks from Mrksic. And as I've already said, all members of OG South command were subordinated commanders who were duty-bound to attend the daily command briefing. In conclusion, therefore, when one deals with this topic, what we submit is this, we submit that Mrksic's position and from the command and control system existing at the time, that he, Mile Mrksic, as commander of OG South had full control of troops that was subordinated to him; he had appropriate troops and sufficient troops in order to take preventative measures or to deal with problematic situations if that became apparent. Not only that, but he also had an obligation to ensure that no such things occurred. Quoting Theunens again, he said: "It was a very strong brigade ... it had the very best manpower." I would like to deal with Mrksic's control over the evacuation of the hospital. On the 18th of November at 0040 hours, OG South received an order from the commander of the 1st Military District, Zivota Panic, and I quote at exhibit 415, tab 8, if the Court would like to turn it up. It's page 2. To: "... take the hospital and the MUP building ... mop-up the remaining Ustasha forces in the liberated parts of the town on the morning of the 19th November by 1000 hours." In a regular combat report sent by the 1st Military District on the 20th of November, Mrksic made a reply. You'll find it in our brief paragraphs 49, 125, 132, and 192, so if I just deal with paragraph -- at tab 9, please. It's highlighted on the first page, one of three, that in actual fact that: "This task was carried out by 1100 hours on the 19th of the 11th and safe movement through town and control protection service were secured." I ask you, please, to reflect on the explanation given by Sljivancanin about why it was that Vance could not visit the Vukovar Hospital, when in actual fact the Vance visit was between 11.00 and I believe 1.00 or close to 2.00 on that very same day. And yet, security reasons were given for that nonattendance by Vance. Again, as we know, there was an agreement, that had been signed, sometimes known as the Zagreb or Evacuation Agreement. We accept clearly that when it was signed, it's difficult sometimes to assess, but clearly there was an intention to do so. There were documents signed. But the important point is that it was an agreement, it was providing the evacuation of the wounded and the sick undergoing medical treatment at the hospital, the agreement also indicated that the hospital would be put under the protection of the International Committee of the Red Cross and clearly the monitors. And on the 19th of November Mrksic was informed of the existence and the content of the evacuation when he met Dr. Bosanac who was clearly the director of the hospital. Bosanac said at transcript page 670: "I told him that an agreement had been signed in Zagreb. On behalf of the Croatian government and on behalf of General Raseta who was representing the JNA, as well as on behalf of the ECMM. This agreement specified the exact modality and route to be taken by the evacuation. I told him that, on the afternoon of the 19th in Negoslavci when we talked." And again, there was confirmation that he was the officer in command in his zone of responsibility. Mrksic actually told Bosanac that it was him who was going to organise the evacuation, and that is confirmed in the evidence of Pringle, where Pringle said that: "The commander could not possibly be unaware of the evacuation because it is a major operation occurring in his area of responsibility. So it is inconceivable that he would be unaware of it. Being aware of it, for the reasons I have just said, I would expect the commander to, with his staff, plan and issue the orders for what is, in effect, a very complex organisation [sic]." That's page 11051. We have heard evidence, and I have already submitted on it, that at the daily command briefing on the 19th of November Mrksic delegated or placed Sljivancanin in charge of the evacuation of the hospital. I repeat the reference that I've already made about Vujic at T 4530 saying that: "Major Sljivancanin said that the hospital was to be vacated according to an evacuation plan and that he, Major Sljivancanin, "would be personally in charge of it." Panic, who was the chief of staff of OG South gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor where he stated as follows. "It was unusual for a security officer to be given the responsibility for an evacuation operation. However, I assume Mrksic appointed Sljivancanin to the position because of the important role the security organ had to play in the operation. Sljivancanin was not only responsible for the selection of the prisoners, he also commanded the entire evacuation of the people to Sremska Mitrovica. This implied that "Sljivancanin was able to issue orders to the military police or any other unit participating in the operation." Well, clearly that is the statement of Panic, and Panic, with the utmost respect to him, went around in circles trying to get away from that statement. But I would ask the Court to look at the way the statement was compiled, to see the methods that were used for the compilation, and the fail-safe devices to ensure that it was accurately recorded. Because Panic, as I said -- he said that the questions were not there, then he said that he perhaps spoke in haste. And what we would submit is that in actual fact that that is incorrect, that he was trying to modify his statement to facilitate Sljivancanin and, to some extent, Mrksic. And when one analyses the taking of the statement, I would submit it is a true statement, because Panic gave a statement or that statement over a three-day period to the officer of the Prosecutor, in July 2005, that's T 14484. When the statement was completed, he did not sign the English copy because he wanted to read it in the Serbian language. And that's at T 14485. In September 2005, two months later, he again met investigators who provided him with a translation of the statement as requested by him in this Serbian language where he read it for two to three hours. He made extensive and detailed corrections on almost every page of the statement. The Court saw them. After all the changes were made, a new copy was printed in the Serbian language and Panic signed each and every page of the statement. Answering one question during his evidence, in reference to an entry in his written statement, Panic stated: "If that's what's written there, that's what I said." And I would submit it is accurate and truthful. May I deal then please with one or two other matters. The Mrksic Defence brief have stated -- team have stated in their closing brief at paragraphs 172 that, based on the 1st Military District command order, Colonel Mrksic got the task for his OG South unit to evacuate the sick, wounded patients in Vukovar Hospital, medical staff together with OG North. There is no written order from Mrksic's superior that is available with regard to the hospital evacuation. It may be said that a logical inference can be made that Mrksic did receive the task of evacuating the hospital from the 1st Military District. In that, that there was an evacuation agreement that was negotiated at a high level, either and both with the military and political hierarchy. Mrksic told Bosanac that he would be in charge of the evacuation and he clearly placed Sljivancanin in charge. Sljivancanin himself told Vujic that he was in charge of the evacuation, and Mrksic issued an order on the morning of the 20th of November tasking his units to proceed with that evacuation. This is reinforced by the fact that it was a high-profile operation such as the evacuation demands careful planning and situation awareness and Mrksic would be expected to exercise tight control and supervision over the responsible commander. That is in the Pringle's report, paragraphs 34 and 68. So therefore, in actual fact, in planning an evacuation, Mrksic would have taken and should have taken a number of factors into consideration, such as the details of the high-level agreement, transportation and escorts, route security and route clearance, security of the evacuees, communication with opposing forces, arrangements and escorts, command and control arrangements, handover and reception arrangements, and administrative arrangements including food, water, and medical support, compliance with the Geneva Convention. However, when one looks at the actual written order itself which is Exhibit 419, you will see that in actual fact it is drafted in very short and very vague terms, and we would submit, bearing in mind Pringle's report, paragraph 70 and Exhibit 419 - I don't have I'm afraid with me - notes that assuming the possibility that such detailed arrangements were ordered orally, that you would expect a record would be noted in the war diary. He also indicated that where there is a record for such arrangements for the Mitnica evacuation on the 18th of November, such record does not appear in the war diary for the 20th of November. And as we have mentioned earlier, you would expect that to contain all matters of importance. In conclusion, therefore, we submit the following: That Mrksic knew of the existence of an evacuation agreement; that he had a briefing with his staff a day prior to the evacuation and distributed tasks, putting Sljivancanin in charge of the entire evacuation; and Mrksic remained responsible for the successful completion of the evacuation, despite the fact that he had delegated it to Sljivancanin himself. Finally, I think we finish at a quarter to 6.00 for the second part, I'd like to deal if I may with the prior knowledge of crimes committed by subordinates for Mr. Mrksic. We would submit that he had prior knowledge of crimes committed by subordinates, included subordinated units such as the TO Petrova Gora and Leva Supoderica during the months of October and November, and that has been extensively covered by us in the Prosecution brief, paragraphs 270 to 293. I would, however, just wish to deal with one incident and that refers clearly to the killings at Ovcara, because on the night of the 19th of November, Vujic was sent by Mrksic and Sljivancanin to monitor the situation at Velepromet. Clearly Vujic went. We submit that he witnessed the violent behaviour of the TO members. He had to use force and threatened to shoot from an APC unless the TO let the prisoners go. And that same night, Vujic returned to OG South command and addressed Mrksic in the following way and the Court will remember quite clearly the words: "Commander, do you have any idea what is going on over there? People killed. This is an attack against the integrity of the JNA. This is an attack against you as a commander. This is an attack against us all. There was a Chetnik duke, as they called him, who wanted to slit my throat in front of all the Ustashas on that bus. That is a disgrace." Now, of course, that is contested and the Court will remember that the evidence of Kolesar was saying that he was with Vujic when he returned; that is not correct. Kolesar said in actual fact that he proceeded Vujic and that he went downstairs to eat. In our submission, again, it comes down to the credibility of Vujic and the assessment of him and I would submit that Vujic is not the sort of man who would say that about a fellow officer if it were not unfortunately true. Might I inquire when Your Honour wishes to rise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] So we shall adjourn for 20 minutes -- half an hour, I'm sorry, because we had to make a redaction. So it will be half an hour. It was an unfortunate mentioning of a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I thank the Court, firstly, for letting us have the day. We will do our very best to finish today, although, I consider and I think with my learned friend that we have about an hour and a half but we will finish by 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There can be only one thing worse than actually speaking a marathon and that is probably listening to it and I will endeavour to ensure that it does not last much longer. I will try and therefore deal with matters in abbreviated form. Clearly the issue of the order to Panic is an important aspect of the case. We say that there is clear evidence that Mrksic ordered Panic to attend the meeting, that he told Panic that he should agree to whatever they decided. We submit that that clearly is an order of enormous importance in relation to consequences, and Mrksic's participation as a member of the joint criminal enterprise. I also seek to pray in aid Vujic's comments on what government they were referring to. Panic's gave evidence. He said that he conveyed Mrksic's order to the local government, my emphasis. "I told them that the commander had told me that he would accept their decision," and that Mrksic's words, when he had been informed by Panic that he had conveyed his order, brief paragraph 422-424, Mrksic had replied: "Let it be as they decided." That's at 14322. So there's clear evidence of ordering, we submit, in relation to that. Surprisingly, in Mrksic's final brief, if I move off topic slightly, at paragraph 491, the Defence submit that Mrksic heard through Panic what was happening at Ovcara. If that is the case, a little surprising we would submit, because it seemed to be that the Defence of Mrksic was suggesting that he did not know and then he was knowing. But in any event, when we deal with Vojnovic, clearly Vojnovic is an important witness. He said that he had spoken to Mrksic at the briefing saying, "Colonel, sir, who are we to do?" Mrksic had replied angle: "Why are you reporting to him on this because he didn't have the time to deal with it?" Vojnovic stating: "I understood it as an order that I shouldn't be there." It's clear that Mrksic does not say by may of Vojnovic: "I order you to withdraw," but the nature of the response, the way that it was said, the conduct of Mrksic in relation to it was clearly an intention by Mrksic to convey to Vojnovic to withdraw the protecting troops and it was an implied order. And Vojnovic himself said: "I understood it as an order that I shouldn't be there." If I may move on again with regard to the Karanfilov situation and Vezmarovic. Vezmarovic said that Karanfilov had told him that there had been a meeting and that he should not be there. In my submission, the important piece of that evidence is at 8437, transcript page, because there Vezmarovic said that saying that I should pull out my units -- I should pull my units back or out, and again that is the conveying of the order at the same time that Mrksic has given the order to Vojnovic. Clearly an officer that is subordinated not only to Sljivancanin but also subordinated to Karanfilov. Panic and also the military expert, Vuga, stated that the order for withdrawal: "Must have been authorised by Mrksic or somebody empowered by him." And the Prosecution submit that almost certainly it was by Sljivancanin who was his direct superior. I will not deal with other points. Alibi. The Defence are stating that alibi plays a part here. In our submission, it doesn't, not when you look at the reality of the case, because it is perfectly clear that if the evidence of Vojnovic is to be believed and Vukasavljevic is to be believed that in actual fact you have the notice given to Mrksic prior to his return to Belgrade, if he went to Belgrade. And there are very significant doubts in our submission about whether that is a genuine alibi. You have also other elements of notice being given to Mrksic. You have evidence from, as I say, Vojnovic; you have got Susic, a Defence witness who said that he told Mrksic about what was occurring; you have Panic, a Defence witness, who said that he told Mrksic what was happening; you have got Tomic via Vujic saying that in actual fact Tomic had told Mrksic what had occurred on two separate occasions and Mrksic had put his hand up to his face; and I would equally submit, the Court are entitled to draw an inference on that because clearly there was a statement and there is no suggestion by the Defence that in actual fact that is inconsistent with what was said in the statement. The Courts are not attracted to that argument; that is entirely a matter for them. But, in our submission, there is evidence in relation to Tomic speaking to Mrksic. Set that aside, you have also Vojnovic, you have Vukasavljevic, and you have Vukasinovic. I see Judge Thelin frowning somewhat. I will repeat the point and it is quite simply this: That Mrksic was told by Susic that he was told by Vukasinovic, Vojnovic, and Vukasavljevic in relation to what was occurring. In relation to the alibi, Mrksic himself accepts that he knew in his Defence brief that Panic had informed him about the trouble. We submit that the alibi evidence is not credible, and, additionally, there is an entry on the 21st of November at 1815 hours that the commander of OG South and a group of officers went to reception by the federal secretary in Belgrade. That's in tab 12, Exhibit 401 and that corresponds, I believe, with Trifunovic who says that Mrksic was present at Negoslavci at the time. We submit that Mr. Mrksic was a participant and was actively involved in the joint criminal enterprise to persecute these individuals and that there is significant evidence which repeats itself that demonstrate that the intention was to kill them. I have other topics that I would wish to deal with, but those would be our submissions in relation to Sljivancanin, Mrksic. May I crave the Court's indulgence on one matter, it is this. My learned friend will be submitting in relation to Radic. If there is any time over, there is a matter that I would like to deal with in relation to 001 and identifications of that topic, but I do not ask to go past 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Mr. Moore, may I ask you a question because you saw us frowning and it's better if I ask it immediately. The Tomic that you mentioned, is that the deceased Mr. Tomic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It is deceased Tomic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Vujic gave evidence of what Tomic had told him and that was the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: But we didn't accept the evidence of Mr. Tomic. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The Court did not accept the evidence of Tomic's statement, but there is nothing in my submission that would necessarily exclude the evidence by way of hearsay as I call it by my definition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon, Your Honours. Your Honours, I will endeavour to cut short the submissions in respect of Miroslav Radic; however, I would say, as a caveat to that, that if there's anything that I omit from my submission or if there's anything that I summarise with a view to finishing within the Prosecution's time-limit, I would certainly refer Your Honours back to the final brief of the Prosecution as a comprehensive document with regard to the Prosecution's position with respect to the guilt of Miroslav Radic. Your Honours, the Prosecution is seeking a conviction of Captain Radic under Article 7(1) or 7(3) of the Statute, and the Prosecution submits at the outset that there is indeed credible and reliable evidence from a number of independent and mutually corroborating sources that allow for this conviction. And there is sufficient evidence covering all eight counts of the indictment. Your Honours will have noted that the closing briefs of the Prosecution and Defence, in relation to Captain Radic, in many respects mirrored each other, dealing with the same points, the same witnesses, and the same evidence. I did not propose obviously, now with the clock ticking, to deal with every area; I now deal with a limited number of points. However, there are two particular points I wish to start with of crucial importance. And one is the facts giving rise to Radic's guilt under 7(1), his act of participation in the joint criminal enterprise, and his identification as participating in that joint criminal enterprise. Your Honours now know that Radic attended Vukovar Hospital in the afternoon of 18th of November, 1991, and whilst the other thought the wounded men as dead men, something that we now know was to transpire, indicating his knowledge of the joint criminal enterprise and indicating his guilt in that regard. He further participated in the joint criminal enterprise later on the 18th and into the 19th of November by participating with Bogdan Kuzmic in the selection process of detainees where detainees were threatened and abused. And my learned friend Mr. Moore has elaborated on that point already. And we know from Dr. Njavro that the objective of that visit was to identify some of the wounded and civilians who would later on the 20th be taken from the hospital and to eventually end up at Ovcara and that Your Honours can be found at page 1525 of the transcript. Radic's participation in the joint criminal enterprise did not end there. He returned on the morning of the 20th, and that morning helped Major Sljivancanin in the selection process as detainees were being loaded on to buses. He further participated in that selection process later that morning at the barracks where he entered one of the buses, read names from a list, and those individuals were then returned back to the hospital. Radic then further participated in this joint criminal enterprise in the afternoon of 20th of November by sending three men to Ovcara to check the information the TO were trying to take the prisoners away, and thereafter reported back to him with regard to that. With regard to those actions, Your Honours, giving rise to liability under Article 7(1), I would submit that the identifications of Radic as participating are provided by witnesses who gave their evidence in a credible and reliable manner and their testimony as such as to allow Your Honours to be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that it was indeed Radic that participated in those actions. In that regard, Your Honours, I would adopt everything that my learned friend Mr. Moore has already said with regard to importance of identification and the standards to be applied. Dealing firstly with witness P16, who identified Radic at the hospital on the 18th of November and the reference to dead men. This, Your Honours, was not simply identification but rather recognition, P016 having obtained it -- the Guards Motorised Brigade barracks on two or three previous occasions in the course of his professional duties. And when he attended Vukovar Hospital on the 18th of November, he was recognising Captain Radic, not simply identifying him. This identification -- rather, this recognition, Your Honours, was corroborated by independent testimony of Dr. Njavro with regard to Radic's attendance on the 18th of November, and in that regard, I would refer to the previous submissions of my learned friend Mr. Moore in respect of the Defence submission on Karan and move forward from there. The Prosecution accepts, Your Honours, that the statement -- the prior statements of the accused are obviously not exhibits in this trial and are not evidence against the accused; however, they were used to test the credibility and the reliability of the accused and, in that regard, Captain Radic was questioned on his two previous testimony. But he confirmed in those statements that he was at the hospital on the 18th of November, 1991, and I would ask Your Honours not to accept the position put forward by the Defence in the final briefs -- final brief, rather, with regard to his explanation given in testimony that he was simply not prepared in the first statement and made a mistake about the 18th of November and that on the second occasion, rather than have an inconsistency, he simply repeated the error. And I should ask Your Honours to bear that in mind when assessing the credibility of Miroslav Radic's denials about attending the hospital on the 18th of November. If I may now move to the identification by witness P030, who identified Captain Radic as participating in the selection process on the morning of 20th of November and assisting Major Sljivancanin in that operation. The Prosecution submits, Your Honours, that that was an accurate identification which can be relied upon confidently by the Trial Chamber. In support of that, Your Honours, it must be remembered that Radic was referred to by name at least four or five times by Sljivancanin as he ordered Radic to search the detainees that morning. This was being between when witness P030 was only 2 to 3 metres away. It was outside in the compound that morning,. It was daylight. Witness P030 told us that Sljivancanin issued these orders and gave a speech for 15 minutes, thus allowing P030 ample time with regard to his identification. And finally with regard to Captain Radic's evidence, he testified that as far as he was aware, there was no one else in the Guards Motorised Brigade by the name of Radic and there was no one else within Vukovar by the name of Radic, to the best of his knowledge. And accordingly, Your Honours should be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that P30 was indeed accurate when describing Captain Radic assisting Sljivancanin in the selection process as part of the joint criminal enterprise. P30 then sees Captain Radic a short time later at the barracks being involved in the selection of detainees off the bus that P30 was on just a short time later and the Prosecution submits that the second identification, now recognition, is equally accurate given the strength of his earlier identification. The defence of Miroslav Radic has suggested that it was only Vukasinovic that attended the buses and took people off the buses. However, Your Honours will recall Vukasinovic's evidence that when he attended, there were three buses there. As we now know, there were five buses and the five buses were then joined by a sixth bus and it was then the reselection process took place. And therefore the testimonies of P30 and Vukasinovic are not mutually exclusive and on that basis it can be inferred that Radic and Vukasinovic, perhaps both participated in that reselection process. The Radic Defence claim that Radic was only at the hospital for a short period of time the morning of the 20th, that he did not enter the building, and did not take any part in the selection process. However, when Radic testified to that set of circumstances, he was asked specifically which officers from the Guards Motorised Brigade or the JNA were present, within the hospital, at that time. And at page 12658 Radic testified that he could only recall Tesic and Pavkovic. There was no mention of Sljivancanin there, of him meeting Sljivancanin, or Radic having any dealings with Sljivancanin. However, Your Honours, the fact that Radic was not only at the hospital on the morning of the 20th but had dealings with Sljivancanin, as corroborated by witness P018, somebody who knew Captain Radic, who recognised him, and indeed attended the hospital with him that morning. And it's important to note, Your Honours, that P18 places Radic not only at the compound but inside the hospital meeting with Sljivancanin and meeting with members of the TO who were inside trying to identify individuals labelled as Ustashas by them. And that, Your Honours, can be found at page 7410 of the transcript. To conclude, Your Honours, on that part of the submission, it is submitted that it is not believable, given the extent and manner of corroborating testimony, that confirms Radic's involvement in the joint criminal enterprise, that Radic knew nothing of this joint criminal enterprise and took no part in it. It is submitted that the Defence position that every witness is wrong or lying or the subject of media influence cannot be correct, cannot be true, given the number of positive identifications and the strength of those identifications. If I can move now, Your Honours, to the intention of Captain Radic, the intention to participate in the joint criminal enterprise as inferred from his actions and knowledge and words. The first evidence the Prosecution would seek to rely upon, Your Honours, is one I already mentioned being the declaration to witness P16 at the hospital that men -- the wounded men on the 18th were dead men was the first indication -- a strong indication of a joint criminal enterprise and the intention of Radic at that time. This is only one of a number of pieces of evidence, and I would refer in general, Your Honours, to the final brief of the Prosecution at part 1, section L, dealing generally with the prior knowledge of the accused and the foreseeability of the crimes and also at part 2, section B of the final brief, which deals specifically with the joint criminal enterprise at paragraphs 37 -- 73 -- 3. Your Honours, Captain Radic has denied any knowledge of plan. He submitted -- rather, the Defence -- paragraph 414 of the Defence brief have submitted that as Captain Radic held the lowest rank within the JNA command structure he was not in receipt of the same information. Your Honours should reject this notion from the outset as simply not true. As a JNA officer, Captain Radic had the same duties of any other officer, to be aware of what was happening in his zone of responsibility, and Your Honours will find that at tab 4 in the binders, Exhibit 394, the JNA textbook on command and control at page 43 in the English and page 33 in the B/C/S. For the sake of brevity, Your Honours, I would not propose to quote verbatim from any of the exhibits, given the lateness of the hour. Your Honours, this -- this duty held by Captain Radic to be aware of what was happening within his zone of responsibility applied to all levels of command, and this is seen within Defence Exhibit 803 at paragraph 23, the Rules for Infantry, Companies, and Platoons, that, Your Honours, can be found at tab 2 in the binder. With regard specifically to the Guards Motorised Brigade, as expert witness Pringle testified at page 11037: "The GMTBR had a well-tried and exercised system of passing information up and down the chain of command." And again with the specifics as to the situation within Vukovar, the Trial Chamber is aware from evidence that Radic did keep himself informed of the situation within his unit. He frequently visited the front line and participated in operations. As Witness P18 testified at page 7395, "But it was through the local Chetniks that he was permanently -- that he was permanently in touch with everyone because they kept informing him of everything." The same people, Your Honours, described as Chetniks by P18 met with Captain Radic within Nova Ulica 81 being the place that Captain Radic set up his -- Prosecution refers to headquarters and my learned friend Mr. Borovic refers to observation post at paragraph 73 to 74 of the final brief of the Prosecution. And I would not propose to go back over that information. Again, just for the sake of completeness of time -- within the time-limit. Moving on, Your Honours, with these factors in mind, with the duties and the evidence as to what the situation was within Vukovar in November 1991, I submit that Radic was fully -- Radic was aware of what was happening within his zone at the time. And with this knowledge, Captain Radic knew that the TO were widely known for their criminal and violent behaviour. He knew that the Leva Supoderica were sponsored by Seselj's Serbian Radical Party, and he knew that that unit of men were particularly violent. Radic knew that Seselj had visited Nova Ulica 81 on November 13th, and Radic was present for the statement referred to by my learned friend: "Not a single Ustasha must leave Vukovar alive." The Defence have suggested, Your Honours, in their final brief, that witness P002 did not testify to Captain Radic being present at that meeting. I would ask Your Honours to reject that submission of the Defence and direct you specifically to page 10382 of the transcript where witness P002 stated that Radic was already in the house that day before the meeting took place, and he further goes on to describe how the officers that he named met with Seselj in the meeting room, the large room within Nova Ulica 81. And it's clear, Your Honours, when you look at that passage as a whole, that P002 indeed places Captain Radic within Nova Ulica 81 on the 13th of November and he places him at that meeting when that statement was being said. The denial of Radic should be rejected with regard to that point and, again, Your Honours, there is of course the corroborating evidence of P22 as to Captain Radic's attendance at Nova Ulica 81 on the 13th of November, when this important statement was made, another statement indicating an intention to kill, intention to murder, a joint criminal enterprise that Captain Radic himself was aware of and willingly participated in for the actions already described. Over and above those matters, Your Honours, Captain Radic was also aware that TO beat and killed Croatian prisoners of war within Nova Ulica at a house across from Nova Ulica 81, and he was further aware of a particular incident described by P22 where one Croatian prisoner of war was beaten by TO in front of Captain Radic. Radic himself confirmed the lawless reputation of Vukovar TO in his interview with journalist Kacarevic which Your Honours will find at tab 20 in the binder as Exhibit 353. The Defence position with regard to that interview, in which Captain Radic refers to the volunteers and those he commanded as adventurers who had come to experience the turmoils of war, looters, and robbers. Your Honours, the Defence position on this interview is contained in paragraphs 444 to 447 of the Defence brief. The Defence take the view that Captain Radic was not prepared for interview and that the interview was not recorded word for word and was later subject to exaggeration for media effect. I would ask Your Honours again to check that submission from the Defence. That matter was never put to witness Kacarevic during his own testimony. Your Honours will recall that the Prosecution and my learned friend and former colleague Mr. Weiner objected to Captain Radic speaking on such matters at page 1265 [sic] -- sorry 685 [sic] of the transcript. And with the matter never put to the witness, I would submit that the Defence's submission is weakened because of that. Witness Kacarevic was never given the opportunity to comment on whether or not he exaggerated or did not record the interview verbatim. And I would ask Your Honours to bear that in mind when weighing up the evidence discussed. Again, Your Honours, with regard to the issue of intent and knowledge, there is the participation I've already described of Radic within the joint criminal enterprise, attending Vukovar Hospital on the 18th, 19th, and 20th of November at a time when witnesses -- sorry, at a time when patients and other persons within the hospital were threatened and mistreated. And again, also the same happening at the barracks where detainees were beaten when they were transferred from one bus to the other at a time when Captain Radic was present. And with all this information, Your Honours, with regard to the reputation and behaviour of the TO and with regard to the situation in Vukovar and the feelings towards Croatian prisoners of war and detainees and those within the hospital specifically, the situation was obvious, the threats were obvious, and indeed the outcome was planned, as per the Prosecution's submission in the final brief. Such was the obvious nature of the dangers of crimes and the particular murder. Even the press were aware of the dangerous situation and took steps to try and cover as much of Vukovar as they could in their capacity as the media to try and prevent any such crimes from taking place. And I simply refer Your Honours to the testimony of Van Lynden in that regard at page 3118 to 3119 of the transcript. Your Honours, to summarise this part of the submission, it's not credible for the Defence of Radic to claim that he was a lowly captain who knew nothing of what was going on around him. It's not credible that Captain Radic did not know of the problems of the TO that formed part of the joint criminal enterprise with him and others. It's not credible that he was not aware of the JCE himself and the role that he himself played within that joint criminal enterprise. And in contrast, Your Honours will be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that Radic was aware of the situation around him. He was aware of the reputation of the TO, he was aware of the joint criminal enterprise and the role that he played in it. If I could move on Your Honours to another aspect of the joint criminal enterprise as provided for in paragraph 10(C) of the indictment, and that is with respect to Captain Radic concealing or hiding the crimes. It's submitted in that regard, Your Honours, that on account of Captain Radic knowing what was going on at the time and thereafter being told about the killings and the immediate aftermath of the killings, that by his omission to report those crimes, formed part of the concealment, as charged in paragraph 10(C) of the indictment. Obviously, Your Honours, there is some common ground in this aspect with 7(3) liability and the failure to punish, and I will address that later, Your Honours, if time permits. As indicated earlier, with regard to Radic's knowledge, he was aware of what was going on on the 20th. He participated at the hospital and barracks and sent three of his own men to confirm that the situation at Ovcara was proceeding as he himself obviously knew. With regard to Radic's actual knowledge of the killings, this comes from two sources, Your Honours. Firstly, the specific reporting to him by a number of individuals; and secondly, with regard to the general widespread rumours circulating in Vukovar in the immediate aftermath of the murders is something my learned friend Mr. Moore has already dealt with in his submission. The Defence position on this knowledge, Your Honours, is two-fold. He submits in his evidence and through the Defence brief that he was not present at Nova Ulica 81 in the evening of the 20th of November when he's allegedly been told about the killings by witnesses P18 and P22, and Radic further denies that regardless of everyone else hearing about these rumours he managed to avoid them and only found out about the killings in the middle of 1992, some seven months later. Your Honours, the Prosecution submits that the alibi with respect to either of the 20th and into the morning of the 21st, this all-night dinner alibi, ought to be rejected at the very outset and it ought to be rejected, Your Honours, for being a lie. Firstly, Your Honours will recall that the dinner alibi was never properly put to the Prosecution witnesses during the course of the trial. And I submit it, Your Honours, that this alibi, with regard to the dinner, was fabricated at a later stage. The Defence witnesses who came to testify about this alleged dinner had no written record, yet still remember details as to the timing, the location, who attended, when they left, and indeed where they sat. The witnesses themselves who spoke about this alibi accepted that they had discussed matters between themselves prior to testifying. However, most importantly, most significantly in respect to this dinner alibi being a false alibi can be seen from the same fatal error that was made by both witnesses, those being Zirojevic and Vuckovic with regard to meeting Tesic the day after the dinner. The Court knows from testimony during the Defence of Mile Mrksic that Tesic did not return to Vukovar from Belgrade until the morning of 22nd of November, 1991, having left very early the day before. This was confirmed by Dusan Milosevic at page 12086 of his testimony. He was a pilot who flew Tesic back in the morning of the 22nd and he refreshed his memory from his flight log. Vuckovic was particularly adamant that he saw and spoke with Tesic the day after the dinner. He recalls this particularly because of Tesic being opposed to drinking, having a dislike for alcohol. And at page 13239, Vuckovic tells us that Major Tesic could see in his face that he partied hard last night and he cannot stand alcohol. This, Your Honours, shows that the alibi cannot be correct. If Tesic arrived -- did not arrive back to Vukovar until the 22nd, then he could not have seen Vuckovic on the 21st to see that he partied hard last night, being the 20th. The Defence deal with this matter at paragraphs 527 to 528 of their final brief and now claim that the date of Tesic's return is irrelevant. The Prosecution submits that's not the case; the date of the return of Tesic is crucial for showing the alibi to be a lie. The Defence final brief at paragraph 527 also seems to shift the position of the witnesses and seems to submit that Tesic arrived the day after the review of the troops that was due to take place in the morning of the 21st, and that clearly was not the case and was not the testimony of Vuckovic at page 13280 when it is clear from the context of his testimony that he met with Tesic on the evening of the 21st. We know, Your Honours, that that could not have taken place because we know Tesic was in Belgrade on the evening of the 21st having attended a reception that day. I submit, Your Honours, in summary with regard to this aspect, that if Captain Radic and two of his key Defence witnesses are prepared to lie on such an important and significant point as to where he was on the evening of the 20th and are prepared to lie with regard to being told about the murders that night, they should not be believed in any aspect, whether it be participation in the joint criminal enterprise or subordination of the TO. Time is pressing on, Your Honours, and I would propose to summarise the rest of the submission in the next five minutes. So far, Your Honours, the Prosecution in respect of Miroslav Radic has attempted to summarise the position with regard to his involvement in a joint criminal enterprise under Article 7(1) and it is submitted that the fall-back position, if Your Honours are not satisfied about his participation, is that at the very least he aided and abetted others to commit the crimes of murder and so on through the indictment with regard to mistreatment of the patients within the hospital, at the barracks, and thereafter at Ovcara. Very briefly with regard to liability under Article 7(3), the Prosecution's submission with regard to subordination is thoroughly set out within the final brief. With regard to Radic's liability for, firstly, his own three soldiers who were present at Ovcara on the 20th of November, two of whom he sent there, P22 and Vidacek, one of whom was already there, Lieutenant Hadzic, his own deputy who filled in for Radic when Radic wasn't present. And thereafter Radic is also guilty under Article 7(3) for the crimes committed by Vukovar TO, the Leva Supoderica, Petrova Gora, who were subordinated to him. Your Honours will be fully aware of the Prosecution's submissions in that regard from the final brief with regard to the eye-witness accounts of Captain Radic having effective de jure -- sorry, de jure and effective de facto control of the soldiers in question of Petrova Gora and the Leva Supoderica. Over and above the eye-witness accounts of this de jure and de facto control is the military theory and practice. The evidence adduced by the Prosecution to confirm that the JNA operated a system of a single command and control, that -- this is provided for within the SFRY law on all people's defence, Exhibit 392 at paragraph 112, that subordination, Your Honours, should be at the lowest possible level as was confirmed by witness Theunens at page 10818 of his testimony. That single structure of command and control was operated on the neighbouring axis of the Zirojevic, as confirmed by him in his own testimony. Even paragraph 122 of the Vuga report of Major Sljivancanin's expert witness confirms that Radic commanded all forces along his units, axis of attack, and in that regard I would direct Your Honours to paragraph 122 of Exhibit 798 at tab 21. Furthermore, with regard to the issue of singleness of command, I would simply remind Your Honours of the testimony of Pringle with regard to the need for strict command and control within an urban warfare setting, that being a particularly difficult area to provide for and Zirojevic himself confirmed that an urban warfare unit of command is difficult to avoid accidents as is stated at page 13167. Moreover, Your Honours, as -- sorry, in contrast to the position put forward by the Defence, Tesic, not Mrksic, were in a position to have direct control, direct de facto effective control of the men in the front line to control their behaviour and issue commands. And accordingly, subordination at the lowest level was necessary in Vukovar to allow the JNA, to allow the GMTBR to operate effectively. And through that, Mrksic from Tesic to Radic and then the Vukovar TO, there was an operation of a single chain of command which gives rise to liability under 7(3) for Mrksic and Radic in that regard. With regard to de facto control, effective control for Radic, I would refer Your Honours to two quotes very briefly P22 at 4984, who testified when talking about the Leva Supoderica, first of all: "Everybody from that unit respected Captain Radic and listened to him, followed his commands," and he repeated that with regard to the Petrova Gora. Thereafter, P24, page 4172 stated: "Through Kameni, the JNA commanded the volunteer units during the war. During the fighting, the role of Kameni as a commander was lost; he was totally irrelevant. Finally, he was a plain soldier, like myself. We all listened to the command of Captain Radic." Your Honours will recall the Defence position through testimony and now from the final brief with regard to there being no subordination between Radic and the TO, and rather, there being a relationship of cooperation or of coordination. I would ask Your Honours to reject that at the outset as being untrue, as being inaccurate, as being not the way the JNA conducted operations. It was indirect -- that proposition is in direct contradiction to the JNA rules as we know were applied in Vukovar at the time, and the Defence submission with regard to the Tesic oral order on or around the 10th to the 12th of November is also not true, because that again goes against JNA regulations as to the recording of important orders dealing with such structure of command and control. There is no record of that oral order ever having been given in either Exhibit 401 or Exhibit 807, being the war diaries of the Guards Motorised Brigade and the 1st Motorised Battalion. And I would ask Your Honours to reject the Defence submissions as being untruthful with regard to -- rather, Radic's position as being untruthful with regard to separation from the Petrova Gora and Leva Supoderica on or around the 10th of November. With regard to 7(3), liability for Radic's failure to prevent, I would simply direct Your Honours to paragraphs 487 to 492 of the brief in respect to knowledge beforehand and with regard to reasonable -- sorry, the necessary and reasonable steps that Captain Radic failed to take as set out in detail at paragraphs 503 to 507 of the Prosecution brief. And similarly, Your Honours, with regard to failure to publish his subordinates, I direct Your Honours to paragraphs to 508 and 510 of the final brief specifying details of the evidence relied upon by the Prosecution with regard to the failure to punish any of his subordinates after the crimes, after he became aware of the killings on the evening of the 20th of November, 1991. And I would add to that part, Your Honours, the submission with regard to his three regular soldiers, P22, Vidacek, and Hadzic, he was told participated in the beatings, with P22 killing three individuals. Captain Radic's 7(3) liability for failing to punish those three individuals is not in any way affected by the Defence position with regard to any separation from the TO on or around the 10th to the 12th of November, 1991. It's now just past 7.00, Your Honours, and to wind up, I would simply submit that Your Honours can be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt of the guilt of Miroslav Radic and accordingly convict him under Article 7(1) for his participation in a joint criminal enterprise or, alternatively, aiding and abetting others to commit the crimes in the indictment or, alternatively, again, Your Honours, under Article 7(3) for the crimes of his subordinates which he knew or had reason to know would take place and yet he took no steps to prevent those crimes from taking place. And secondly, after he heard about them, after he was told in the night of the 20th and in the morning of the 21st by P022, he did nothing within the period of the indictment to take any steps to punish the perpetrators of those crimes. I would ask Your Honours to bear in mind the false alibi of Radic with -- also ask Your Honours to bear in mind the denials of knowledge with regard to the JCE, the reputation of the TO, the Seselj visit. The Defence are suggesting to Your Honours that Captain Radic knew nothing. He was blindfolded in Vukovar for the six -- eight weeks he was there fighting and he seemed to miss all this information which we have heard from so many other witnesses that they were aware of the problems, of the crimes that were being committed, of the reputation of the TO. In contrast to that, Your Honours, I would ask the Trial Chamber to accept the evidence put forward by the Prosecution witnesses as credible and liable and Your Honours can indeed be satisfied of the guilt of Captain Radic beyond a reasonable doubt. I propose to say nothing further at this stage, unless there's anything else that I can be assistance of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Mr. Moore, that we have run out of time, so we have to adjourn for the day and we will resume tomorrow at a quarter past 2.00. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my apologies for taking up several seconds more, but if this is the conclusion of the closing argument of the OTP, I think they still owe us what they wrote in their final brief, their sentencing submissions. I'm not sure if we'll hear that tonight, but we might actually prefer to hear that tonight as opposed to tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I deal with it very quickly? It's not to do with sentencing. What I was going to suggest was that perhaps it could be dealt with at the conclusion of the arguments on Friday; that had been my intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: That is what I was going to suggest as well, at the end of the brief of Mr. Lukic. Is there -- would the Defence have any problem with that or would you prefer, Mr. Moore, to address this tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it might be technically better to do it now because then the Defence would have an opportunity to address the issue in our own closing arguments. That would shorten the procedure, and we can find it easier to incorporate our own positions in our final arguments. I think our clients -- I think the other teams would also prefer to know tonight so that they might be better able to prepare for their closing arguments, as long as that is no problem, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: I'm afraid it is a problem in view of the tapes and in view of the fact that the accused have to be brought back to the UNDU. So I'm turning now to Mr. Moore to ask how much time would you need for these submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would have thought not a long time. Perhaps the best way of dealing with it, if the Court agrees, is that I can speak to my learned friends now. I can speak to them tomorrow morning because we don't start until quarter past 2.00. I, from my part, don't think the sentencing elements will take any significant amount of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Do you have an assessment because we really have to plan our time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, planning time, I would have said no more than 15 minutes for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll start with that tomorrow at a quarter past 2.00 and we'll make sure that by 2.30 the Defence can start. Is that in agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you. So we adjourn now for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 15th day of March, 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 25
